result.summary: The cause is confirmed. In the rank-16 bridge space, two unrelated asks from the same chat have a mean cosine of 0.308. That is almost as high as an ask's 10th-best node key (0.350) and well above the mean ask-to-node cosine (0.100). As a result, 40% of unrelated asks would push an alias into another ask's top 10, while only 1.1% of ask pairs share evidence. The raw alias rule (0.463, reproduced exactly) fills 7.1 of every 10 top slots with new false positives, all of them on aliased nodes. Of the fixes, the CSLS hub correction failed (0.609 with clean cites). A plain margin (0.671) and storing the action-side view of the ask (0.674) recover most of the loss. The additive hub-corrected bonus (score = k.s + beta*max(0, a.s - r_K(a))) does best: 0.686 alone, 0.687 when combined with the action view. Both beat the 'move' rule with clean cites (+0.008/+0.009 paired, CI excludes 0) and degrade more gracefully. At 30% wrong cites they score 0.675/0.676 against move's 0.657. At 60% wrong they score 0.660/0.664, at or above the baseline, against move's 0.633. In the self-loop they score 0.654/0.656, against the 0.657 baseline and move's 0.634. So a fixed alias rule matches or beats move at every cite condition. Under self-loop and 60% noise it only avoids harm and adds no gain.

caveats: Diagnostic (mean over the 10 test chats, each scored with its own fold's bridge): unrelated asks in the same chat have a mean cosine of 0.308, against 0.152 across chats, 0.100 for ask-to-node, 0.379 for an ask to its own evidence, and 0.350 for an ask's 10th-best key. An alias made from an unrelated ask enters the top 10 in 40.4% of pairs (88.4% when the pair shares evidence), but only 1.1% of ask pairs share evidence, so nearly every alias that enters is a false positive. With the action-view alias the unrelated entry rate falls to 5.8%. The mechanism is best described as a scale mismatch: asks in one chat resemble each other through shared names and question templates, more than they resemble nodes. It is not hubness in the narrow sense of a few nodes winning for everything. Ask-ask cosine does carry real signal (AUC 0.874 for sharing evidence vs not), so the information is there once it is calibrated.

Raw alias failure reproduced exactly: 0.463 with clean cites. Its top 10 holds 7.1 new false positives per ask, all on aliased nodes, and recall falls with visit position (0.498, 0.428, 0.462 by third, against the baseline's 0.649, 0.677, 0.647).

F2 (CSLS on both keys and aliases) failed at every K and every cite condition, with about 5.5 new false positives per ask. Its keys-only control is neutral (+0.004, CI includes 0). Likely reason, not verified: the CSLS score doubles the alias term, so the wide ask-ask cosine distribution still wins, and r(a) is a fixed per-alias offset that cannot remove the per-query tail.
Under self-loop and at 60% wrong cites, the fixed alias rules only avoid harm. They land at baseline (-0.006 to +0.007) instead of move's -0.023/-0.024; they add no gain there.

The 'move eta=0.1' reference comes from e6 and was not tuned here. Move tuned on dev with the same 4-condition criterion picks eta 0.02. That makes it more robust (at baseline under noise and self-loop) but weaker with clean cites (0.666). Even on dev, move's best clean-cite score (0.665 at eta=0.1) stays below F3's (0.684), so the alias-bonus advantage is not an artifact of uneven tuning.
Under BM25 reciprocal-rank fusion almost all differences vanish: lowrank+bm25 0.656, move 0.661, F3 0.662, F5 0.661, and even raw alias 0.649. The learning gains are a dense-only result.

Headline CIs use the e6-style iid visit bootstrap, which treats the 3 visit orders of a question as independent. Question-cluster bootstrap CIs (in the notes and run2.log) are wider but change no conclusion. There are only 10 chats and 5 folds, so no chat-level CI is reported.

Dev tuning used only 2 dev chats per fold, and the chosen settings varied by fold (F1 margin 0.2 to 0.5; F3 beta and K varied). Move and CSLS picked grid edges (eta 0.02, K=3). The grid was widened once, after fold 0's dev-only tuning, before any test result existed. The aborted first run is in /tmp/claude-0/sm/fix-alias-hub/run1.log.

Disclosure: before writing the script I ran a throwaway probe of cosine statistics on test chats 0 to 3 with the fold 0/1 bridges. It used evidence only to label pairs for measurement. It may have shaped the grid ranges (margin sizes), but no setting was selected from it; selection was dev-only. The probe files were deleted.

Cite noise here uses common random numbers, so all rules see the same coin flips. e6 shared one rng stream across arms instead, so the noisy move numbers differ slightly from e6 (0.657 vs 0.654 at 30% wrong; 0.633 vs 0.634 at 60%; 0.634 self-loop in both).

F3 and F5 are statistically indistinguishable; the action view adds little once the hub-corrected bonus is used. The hub reference set is the training chats' ask states plus earlier asks of the same chat, never current or future ones. An alias never counts its own ask.

result.summary: I tested 9 memory-plane learning rules against the rank-16 baseline (0.657) with no learning. Each ran with clean cites, 30% and 60% wrong cites and self-loop, plus three audit conditions not used for tuning. No rule keeps the full gain while staying harmless everywhere, and none gains from self-loop. Two come close. Pull-plus-push 'contrastive' (pull cited nodes, push opened-but-not-cited top-10 nodes away) scores +0.026 clean, +0.014 at 30% wrong, +0.003 at 60% (CI spans 0) and -0.005 on self-loop (CI [-0.011,+0.000]). The pre-registered 'combo' (centered pull + BM25 agreement + small centered push) scores +0.018 / +0.009 / +0.000 / -0.001 and stays positive on the harder audit noise. E6's 'move' rule reproduces exactly (+0.020 / -0.003 / -0.024 / -0.023). The simulated verifier on top of move cuts the 60% harm to -0.002 and the self-loop harm to -0.011. All gains shrink to +0.006 or less once BM25 is fused in, and to +0.005 to +0.009 when cites are limited to what was actually opened.

caveats: No rule gains from self-loop. The best are neutral: combo -0.001 [-0.005,+0.004], and surprise exactly 0.000 only because it never learns from a rank-1 cite. Under 60% wrong cites the best rules are about 0 (contrastive +0.003, CI spans 0), not a gain.

Peek disclosure: before the full run I did a 1-fold, 1-order smoke run that printed fold-0 test numbers. Arms, grids and the tuning objective were not changed after it. The only later edits were an algebraically identical speedup of the slow adapter (dual form of the ridge solve, checked to 2e-13 against the primal) and printing per-chat counts. The rerun reproduced every number exactly.

Multiple comparisons: 10 arms x 7 conditions with no correction. The ci_low/ci_high fields are e6-style visit-level paired bootstraps, which ignore that the 3 orders of a question are correlated. The stricter question-cluster CIs are in each arm's notes and are about 30% wider. Gaps between the top arms (contrastive vs centered vs combo vs verifier+combo) are within noise.

The surprise rule exploits the noise model. E6 draws wrong cites only from the top-10, and self-loop cites only rank 1, so down-weighting high-ranked cites filters them by construction. In the far60 audit, where wrong cites come from the top-50, it falls to -0.017 [-0.024,-0.011], as bad as plain move. Do not adopt it on this evidence.

The oracle 'clean' cites include evidence outside the opened top-10, which a real reasoning plane would never have seen. With cites limited to opened nodes ('visible' audit), plain move gains nothing (-0.002) and the best rules give only +0.005 to +0.009 (contrastive +0.008, slow-adapter +0.009, combo +0.005). This is the more realistic size of the effect.
All gains are dense-only. With BM25 reciprocal-rank fusion the baseline is 0.656 and no rule adds more than +0.006.

The noise model is idealised: a wrong cite is a uniform non-evidence pick from the top-10 (top-50 in the audit), independent of question difficulty. A real LLM probably errs on the most plausible distractor and on hard questions, which could hurt more. The verifier is simulated with independent errors (catch 0.7, false drop 0.1). Real verifier errors correlate with the hard cases, so the verifier arms are optimistic. Under self-loop the verifier is an outside signal, so verifier arms there are not 'no outside signal'.

agree-bm25 alone did cut wrong cites (350 vs 2049 learned at 30%). It also threw away more than half of the correct cites, so the clean gain fell to +0.004 (not significant). It is useful only inside the combo, where dev tuning often switched it off (agree=off in 2 of 5 folds).

The slow adapter (ridge regression of k_v - s on s, refit every 10 asks) is the closed-form MSE version of candidate (4), not an InfoNCE refit, chosen for runtime. It lowers multi-hop recall relative to the key-moving rules (clean 0.478 vs about 0.50).

The centered rule and combo use a running mean of this chat's ask vectors seen so far: question text only, never evidence, with a prior of 10 pseudo-asks at the training-chat mean. Motivation: the mean ask vector has norm about 0.75, so plain move turns cited nodes into hubs.
LoCoMo evidence labels are incomplete. Pushing opened-but-not-cited nodes in the clean condition may push turns that are relevant but unmarked, and scoring uses the same incomplete labels.

Dev tuning per fold uses only 2 dev chats (about 300 questions), so the chosen settings vary across folds (see notes). There is one bridge training seed per fold, as in e6. Common random numbers: every arm sees the same swap and verifier draws per (chat, order, question). The swapped-in wrong node still depends on each arm's own current top-10, as in e6.

The script uses the encoder-output cache /tmp/claude-0/sm/fix-cite-noise/chats.pkl (13 MB), produced by e5_bridges.load in this session; the LoCoMo SHA-256 is checked. Delete the cache to re-encode from scratch. The baseline 0.657 and move clean 0.678 match E6 exactly; move's noisy and self-loop numbers match E6 within 0.001.

Dev chats are (2f+2)%10 and (2f+3)%10, which are training chats. The inner bridge never sees the dev or test chats. Every arm runs on the same orders (e6 seeds) and the same cite draws, the bootstrap is paired per visit, and the BM25/fusion code matches e6. Each run_chat builds a fresh Plane, so no state passes between arms.

I re-implemented the hub scores r(k) and r(a) by brute force, recomputed from scratch at every visit and excluding each alias's own ask (/tmp/claude-0/sm/fix-alias-hub/verify/check_plane.py). The scores match the script's incremental Plane to within 2.4e-7 for bonus, csls, action-view bonus and margin.

The numbers reproduce exactly. I re-encoded from scratch rather than using chats.pkl, and the fresh encodings are bit-identical to the cache. results.json differs by 0 on every arm, the diagnostics and per-fold choices are identical, and the baseline, clean move, raw alias and self-loop arms match e6_result.txt down to the per-category numbers. Log: /tmp/claude-0/sm/fix-alias-hub/verify/verify_run.log.

Overstated statistically: F3 and F5 beat move eta=0.1 with clean cites by +0.008 and +0.009 only under the e6-style iid visit bootstrap. With a chat-cluster bootstrap over the 10 test chats the CIs include 0: F3 +0.0065 [-0.0036,+0.0153], 8 of 10 chats positive; F5 +0.0070 [-0.0049,+0.0177]. Against the baseline the gains hold at chat level: F3 +0.028 [+0.017,+0.038] and F5 +0.028 [+0.015,+0.041], each positive in 9 of 10 chats.

The 'degrades more gracefully than move' margins (+0.027/+0.031 at 60% wrong cites, +0.020/+0.022 in the self-loop) are measured against move eta=0.1, which the same dev protocol would not choose. Against dev-tuned move (eta mostly 0.02) the margins are much smaller. At 60% wrong: F3 +0.005 [+0.0003,+0.009], F5 +0.009 [+0.005,+0.014]. Self-loop is a tie: F3 +0.001 [-0.003,+0.004], F5 +0.003 [-0.000,+0.007], with chat-level CIs also including 0. With clean cites the gap over tuned move is larger (+0.021) and survives chat-level resampling. 'Matches or beats move at every condition' is therefore true, but under noise and in the self-loop it amounts to roughly a tie with properly tuned move.

Minor: in the JSON, F3 self-loop has ci_high = 0, but the log shows -0.004 [-0.007,-0.000]. F4 self-loop is [-0.004,-0.000], and F1 is -0.006 at both 60% wrong and self-loop, with CIs excluding 0. These are small but statistically real harms at visit level, not just 'avoids harm' (chat-level CIs include 0 for F3 and F4).

Soft and unverifiable: the disclosed throwaway probe of cosine statistics on test chats 0 to 3 may have shaped the grid ranges. Selection itself was dev-only and the grids are broad. The widened grid (run1.log) is consistent with the explanation that fold 0's dev tuning picked grid edges, and no test output appears in run1.log.

The mechanism claim is supported, but by correlation plus intervention rather than proven. Unrelated same-chat asks have cosine 0.308, against 0.350 for an ask's 10th-best key, and 40.4% of them would enter the top 10. Raw alias adds 7.09 new false positives per ask, all on aliased nodes. Calibrating the alias term (margin, action view, hub-corrected bonus) removes most of them. The agent's relabeling from hubness to 'scale mismatch' is accurate.
result.bottom_line: Confirmed. The code is sound: there is no leakage, the comparisons are paired on the same visits as e6, and the hub-score bookkeeping matches a brute-force recomputation. Every number reproduces exactly, including after re-encoding from scratch. Raw alias collapses (0.463) because unrelated same-chat asks score almost as high as an ask's 10th-best node (0.308 vs 0.350), so aliases flood the top 10 with false positives. The hub-corrected additive bonus (F3 0.686, F5 0.687) is a real gain over the 0.657 baseline (chat-level CI about [+0.016,+0.040], 9 of 10 chats positive). Three caveats. (1) The clean-cite win over move eta=0.1 (+0.008/+0.009) does not survive a chat-cluster bootstrap (CIs include 0). (2) Against dev-tuned move, the margins at 60% wrong cites are only +0.005/+0.009, and the self-loop is a tie. (3) In the self-loop F3 does slight but CI-significant harm at visit level (-0.004), rather than only avoiding harm. result.summary: I tested three vector-only versions of the read-again loop against the low-rank bridge, which reproduced at 0.657 with multi-hop at 0.475. None of them fixed multi-hop. The learned hop bridge lowered recall@10 by 0.012 overall and 0.017 on multi-hop. The two untrained second hops that average the ask with the hop-1 node lowered it by 0.023 to 0.027. Restricting search to the 3 best BM25 sessions (pyramid) raised overall recall by 0.025, almost all from single-hop questions (0.703 to 0.813), but cut multi-hop by 0.134, because only 43% of multi-hop evidence sits in those 3 sessions. The hop fails even when its start is right: hop 1 hits evidence on only 33% of multi-hop questions, and on the 92 where it does, the learned hop adds just +0.002.

result.tuning: The low-rank baseline and the bridge under every arm are trained exactly as in e6 (40 epochs, rank 16, seed = fold). The untrained hops were fixed in advance as two settings with plain fusion (w=1), and both are reported: hop-avg-key averages in bridge space, hop-avg-enc averages in encoder space and passes the result through the state head. The pyramid's settings (3 sessions, BM25) came from the task. The learned hop head was tuned only on training chats. In each outer fold, the 8 training chats were split into 4 dev pairs. For each pair, a bridge and the hop heads were trained on the other 6 chats and scored on the pair. The grid was rank {4,16} x epochs {20,60} x training pairs {gold, gold+top1} x fusion weight w {0.5,1.0}. The setting with the best pooled overall dev recall@10 was retrained on all 8 chats and run once on the 2 test chats. Chosen settings: fold 0 r16/e60/gold+top1/w0.5; folds 1-3 r4/e60/gold+top1/w0.5; fold 4 r4/e60/gold/w1.0. On dev the best hop never beat the low-rank bridge by more than 0.002 (dev lowrank vs best hop: .648/.650, .642/.633, .654/.651, .637/.637, .662/.663). The winners sit at the edge of the grid (least hop weight, most epochs), meaning the best setting was the one that hops least. Test-chat evidence was used only for scoring.

caveats: Negative result for the read-again loop in vector-only form. Every second-hop arm lowered multi-hop recall, and the CIs exclude zero. The learned head only reduced the damage that the untrained average does.

Why the hop fails: hop 1 (low-rank top-1) is an evidence turn for only 36% of all questions and 33% of multi-hop ones. Even when it is right, the second hop adds at most +0.009 on multi-hop. So the vectors ask + hop-1 node carry almost no second-hop signal; a noisy hop 1 is not the only problem. A real reasoning plane that writes a new query (an entity, a bridging fact) is not tested here.

The pyramid helps overall only through single-hop and 'when' questions. It hurts multi-hop badly because multi-hop evidence spreads across sessions: only 42.7% of it falls in the 3 BM25 sessions. Fusing the pyramid list with BM25 drops it to 0.632.

The pyramid|lowrank arm (+0.058 overall, -0.057 multi-hop) was added after the first test run. It has no tuned parameters, but its design was chosen after seeing that run's test results, so it needs confirmation on new data or under a fresh pre-registration.

CIs are paired bootstraps over the 1531 unique questions; with no key learning, each question is scored once. e6 counted each no-learning visit 3 times, which narrows its CIs by about sqrt(3), so its intervals and mine are not directly comparable. Questions within a chat are correlated, and a question-level bootstrap ignores that, so all CIs here are still somewhat optimistic.

Dev selection maximised overall recall@10, not multi-hop recall; selecting on multi-hop was not tried. The 'gold+top1' training pairs take the bridge's in-sample top-1 on training chats, which is right more often than at test time, so training only partly matches the hop-1 errors seen at test.

The hop head scores against the frozen bridge keys: there is no separate hop action head and no node-to-ask InfoNCE term. Hop-2 lists keep the hop-1 node first, then fuse with the hop-1 list by RRF (k=60).

For pyramid+hop, the split by whether hop 1 was right uses the global low-rank top-1, not the top-1 inside the opened sessions, so that diagnostic (in run2.log and results.json) is only a rough indication.

Encoder outputs are cached in /tmp/claude-0/sm/fix-second-hop/chats.pkl, written by this script's own call to load(); the script checks the LoCoMo SHA before using it. Turn-to-session mapping comes from re-reading /tmp/locomo10.json; there are no duplicate dia_ids, and every dia_id prefix matches its session_N.

issues: The code has no bugs or leakage that I could find. I read fix_cite_noise.py line by line. Each visit is scored before its own cites are made. Cites, the verifier and pushes only use the current question's evidence after it is scored, so they only affect later visits. The running ask mean uses question text only, and mu0 comes from training chats only. BM25 positions and the agree filter use question text only. Dev tuning (dev = the test pair of fold f+1, with the dev bridge trained on the other 6 chats) never touches the test chats, and the audit conditions are not in the tuning objective. The baseline runs on the same test_cases, orders and keys as every arm. The bootstrap is paired over identical visits, and the meta/qid/category arrays line up with the concatenation order. RRF matches e5 fuse, including tie-breaking.

Leakage perturbation test (verify/leak_test.py), using the script's own run_chat. I swapped the evidence of the question visited at position k = 5, 40 and 120, keeping the same count so the shared random streams don't change. Across all 10 arms, all 7 conditions and the baseline (213 checks), recall and hybrid recall of every earlier visit stayed bit-identical (0 failures). Positive control: recall at visit k always changed, and later visits changed for some arms, so the test is live.
Encoder cache: the shipped chats.pkl is bit-identical to a fresh e5_bridges.load encode (max abs diff 0.0; same ids, docs, text and qs; 1531 questions; LoCoMo SHA matches).

Reproduction: I ran a copy from a fresh encode (verify/fix_cite_noise_copy.py; the only changes are an explicit sys.path for -I and the cache filename). All 5 folds tuned to identical per-fold settings, and the whole result table (71 rows, every arm x condition, CIs, q-CIs, +bm25, learned counts, per-chat signs) is textually identical to run.out. All 71 claimed JSON rows match results.json to 4 decimals.

Independent re-implementation (verify/indep_check.py, which imports nothing from the claimed script; move uses E6's own Plane). It matches the claim to 4 decimals on every deterministic condition. Baseline 0.6573 / multi-hop 0.4749 / +bm25 0.656. Move: clean 0.6777, self 0.6341, visible 0.6549. Contrastive: 0.6831 / 0.6524 / 0.6657. Centered: 0.6807 / 0.6521 / 0.6610. Combo: 0.6756 / 0.6566 / 0.6626. With a different RNG (E6-style), the noisy conditions land within about 0.002: contrastive wrong30 +0.0155 vs claimed +0.0141, wrong60 +0.0033 vs +0.0031; combo wrong30 +0.0093 vs +0.0094, wrong60 -0.0003 vs +0.0001; move wrong30 -0.0033 vs -0.0029, wrong60 -0.0260 vs -0.0242. Noisy-condition point estimates therefore carry about ±0.002 of draw noise on top of the CIs.

Minor factual imprecision: the caveat and docstring say the mean ask vector has norm about 0.75. That holds for the raw encoder asks (0.72 to 0.76 per chat). The bridge state vectors that move and centered actually pull toward have mean norm 0.45 to 0.60 (fold-0 bridge). The de-hubbing motivation still holds qualitatively, but the number describes the wrong space.

Wording: the summary's 'gains shrink to +0.005 to +0.009 when cites are limited to what was opened' applies only to the best three rules (contrastive +0.008, slow-adapter +0.009, combo +0.005). Under 'visible', move is -0.002, verifier+move -0.002, agree-bm25 0.000, move-tuned and surprise +0.001, verifier+combo +0.002, centered +0.004. The caveat states this correctly; the summary line is loose.

Statistical caveats (disclosed, and they hold up): there are 70 arm x condition cells with no multiplicity correction. The visit-level CIs ignore that the 3 orders of a question are correlated. Several small 'significant' audit effects lose significance under the question-cluster CI: combo far60 +0.005 and visible +0.005, contrastive far60 and visible go from a lower bound of +0.002/+0.004 to +0.001, and centered self goes to [-0.011,+0.000]. Contrastive self-loop at -0.0049 [-0.0105,+0.0001] is borderline, so calling it 'not harmless' is a judgment call. The claim's conservative framing is reasonable.

Design caveats, disclosed and not bugs: the clean-condition push uses oracle non-evidence labels for the opened top-10. The verifier is simulated from ground truth with independent errors, which makes it an outside signal under self-loop. Surprise's robustness is an artifact of drawing wrong cites from the top-10 (it fails in the far60 audit). Part of contrastive's noise robustness comes from the smaller tuned pull step (eta 0.05 vs move's 0.1), although it also beats move-tuned. The fold-0 test-number peek from the smoke run cannot be verified from the artifacts, but tuning is nested on training chats only, so it could have influenced at most the arm and grid design.
result.bottom_line: Confirmed: the claim holds. I found no leakage or bugs. The 213 evidence-perturbation checks and a code read show test evidence is used only for scoring and for later visits' feedback, and tuning touches training chats only. A fresh-encode rerun reproduced every number, every tuned setting and the whole results table exactly. An independent re-implementation matches all deterministic conditions to 4 decimals, and the noisy ones within about 0.002. The substance stands. Contrastive pull+push gives +0.026 clean and +0.014 at 30% wrong; combo is about neutral on self-loop and 60% wrong. No rule gains from self-loop. Gains drop to at most +0.006 with BM25 fused and to at most +0.009 with opened-only cites. Only nits: (1) the '~0.75 mean ask norm' describes raw encoder asks, not the bridge states the rules pull toward (0.45 to 0.60); (2) the summary's '+0.005 to +0.009 visible' covers only the top three rules; (3) several small audit effects are not significant under the question-cluster CI. Files are in /tmp/claude-0/sm/fix-cite-noise/verify/: run_repro.out and results.json (the rerun), indep_check.py and indep.out, leak_test.py and leak_test_pos.py, cmp_cache.py, check_claim_vs_results.py, side_checks.py.

issues: No leakage found. Test-chat evidence is used only for scoring and for diagnostics. There is no cite feedback at all, because no arm learns keys. Bridge and hop-head training, the gold and gold+top1 pairs, and the inner CV in select() all use the outer fold's 8 training chats only. Session opening (BM25 over session tokens) uses only the question text.

The baseline matches e6 exactly. Same train() call (40 epochs, rank 16, seed = fold, same chat order). train() reseeds itself, so the order heads are trained in does not matter. Same stable argsort of keys @ states. Every arm is scored on the same 1531 questions, and the bootstrap is paired (d = arm - lowrank per question). BM25 (k1 1.2, b 0.75) and RRF (k 60) are standard, and wfuse equals fuse when w = 1.

Reproduction is exact. The unchanged copy (verify/second_hop.py) re-encoded everything from scratch instead of using the pickle and printed a log identical to run2.log in every result line. The fresh encodings equal chats.pkl bit for bit (max abs diff 0.0; ids, qs and docs identical). My independent re-implementation (verify/indep_check.py) maps sessions from the dia_id prefix instead of the session_N keys. It rebuilds the learned hop from the per-fold choices and matches all arms to 3 decimals. The cache check only verifies the JSON's SHA, not the pickle, but this has no effect because the encodings are identical.

The CIs are a little optimistic, as the author warns. In a chat-level (cluster) bootstrap I ran, the pyramid's overall gain of +0.025 has CI [-0.000, +0.050], and 4 of the 10 test chats lose recall. Treat the 'pyramid raises overall recall' finding as fragile. hop-avg-key's multi-hop CI is [-0.052, -0.001], which barely excludes zero. Under the cluster bootstrap the other conclusions hold: hop-avg-enc [-0.039, -0.016], hop-learned [-0.020, -0.003] overall and [-0.031, -0.003] multi-hop, pyramid multi-hop [-0.164, -0.100], pyramid|lowrank [+0.040, +0.074]. The last one is post-hoc, and the author flags that.

Minor wording problem. '75.7% of all evidence / 42.7% of multi-hop evidence in the 3 opened sessions' are per-question averages of the share of evidence inside. Counted over all evidence turns instead, the shares are 64.1% and 39.7%. The conclusion is the same: multi-hop evidence spans 2.68 sessions on average, and 17% of multi-hop questions span more than 3.

Minor misreading. 'Winners at the grid edge (least hop weight, most epochs) mean the best setting hops least' is wrong about epochs: 60 epochs means more training, not less hopping. Because the winners sit at the edge, I ran a check on the training chats only (verify/dev_edge.py) with 200 epochs over the rest of the grid. It never beats dev lowrank by more than 0.002 (fold 3: 0.639 vs 0.637; the other folds are equal or worse). The edge of the grid does not change the negative result.
'Almost all from single-hop' understates it. Single-hop alone adds about +0.060 to overall recall; 'when', inference and multi-hop take back about 0.035, which leaves +0.025.

Extra diagnostic that supports the causal claim. I gave the hop an oracle start: hop 1 set to each gold turn of questions with 2 or more evidence turns, scored on the remaining evidence, with that turn removed from both lists. Multi-hop recall@10 was 0.427 for the plain ask state, 0.426 for hop-avg-key, 0.429 for the learned head, and 0.442 when the hop list is fused with the plain list. The ask plus hop-1 node vectors carry almost no second-hop signal even when hop 1 is right. This is stronger evidence than the author's 92-question split, which is a selected, easier subset.
result.bottom_line: Confirmed. The code has no leakage, and the baseline is identical to e6's bridged-lowrank. I re-ran an unchanged copy with a fresh encoder load (verify/verify_run.log) and every number matched run2.log exactly. An independent re-implementation (verify/indep_check.py) matched to 3 decimals too. The negative result holds: no vector-only second hop raises multi-hop recall, and an oracle-start check shows the hop carries almost no signal even when hop 1 is a gold turn. Two caveats. The pyramid's overall gain of +0.025 is fragile, with chat-level bootstrap CI [-0.000, +0.050]. pyramid|lowrank (+0.058) is post-hoc and needs fresh confirmation. There are also small wording errors (the shares are per-question averages, and the 'grid edge means hop least' reading is wrong). A dev-only 200-epoch check showed the edge of the grid does not change the result. Files are in /tmp/claude-0/sm/fix-second-hop/verify/.

errors.claim: Verdict: 'What nobody has shown yet is this: bridges that are open, cheap to fine-tune, and trained from the reasoning plane's own feedback, on a memory that also learns its own structure.'
errors.correction: This overstates the gap. RMM (Tan et al., ACL 2025) already puts small trainable heads on a frozen retriever. Each side gets a residual linear adapter (q' = q + W_q q, m' = m + W_m m) scored by dot product. The heads are trained online with REINFORCE from the answering LLM's own citations: cited memories score +1 and retrieved-but-uncited ones score -1. That is almost exactly the page's 'cited = positive, opened-but-unused = hard negative' backward pass, and RMM's memory also has several granularities (utterance, turn and session topics). On structure: HAGE learns edge structure from downstream reward, and REALM (Sep 2026) rewires graph topology after each retrieval based on answer feedback, though by prompting an LLM agent rather than with learned heads. What is genuinely still open is narrower: a contrastive (InfoNCE) head family covering read, stop, write, reshape and forget; learned rather than prompted topology operations; per-node alias keys; and joint LoRA training. Note also that the page's current results use the benchmark's gold evidence as 'oracle cites', so they do not yet show training from the reasoning plane's own feedback.

errors.claim: HAGE row: 'Closest to our backward pass; we add contrastive training on cites and learned structure.' Problem it hit: 'RL variance.'
errors.correction: HAGE already learns structure. Every edge has a trainable relation-feature vector, optimised together with the router by REINFORCE (with an exponential-moving-average baseline) from downstream reward. What HAGE lacks is topology change (split, merge, new nodes) and learned node keys. Its reward is gold-evidence hits: target nodes are found by matching node content against the ground-truth answers. That is the same supervision as the page's current 'oracle cites'. HAGE also uses a frozen small encoder (all-MiniLM-L6-v2) and 5-fold cross-validation over LoCoMo conversations, the same held-out-chats protocol the page uses. 'RL variance' is the page's own inference, not a problem HAGE reports. HAGE's stated limitations are its dependence on the LLM intent classifier and on the LLM judge. The 'LLM classifier in the loop' point is correct.
errors.source: https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.09942 (sections 3.4 and 4.1, Limitations; full text at https://arxiv.org/html/2605.09942)

errors.claim: Jev-Mem row: 'Jev is closed and zero-shot, so the controller cannot learn from use.' Verdict: 'Jev-Mem (September 2026) puts a fast decision model between an LLM and a graph memory.'
errors.correction: Essentially correct, with caveats that matter. Jev is TypeSafe AI's proprietary API model. Jev-Mem calls it zero-shot through typed prompts ('Nouls' and 'Choice' via TypeSafeClient.system_one, listed in Appendix B), and the paper trains no controller. However, Jev-Mem's own code is public (github.com/libingzheren/Jev-Mem), so 'closed' applies only to the Jev model. CLM-8B exposes the same system_one / Noul / Choice interface and claims zero-shot parity with Jev, so swapping in an open, fine-tunable controller is close to a drop-in change, which weakens 'open' as a point of novelty. The 0.777 score was submitted 21 Sep 2026. It is a LoCoMo-only, gpt-4o-mini, LLM-as-judge number: the paper says 'two benchmarks' but reports only LoCoMo. Jev-Mem comes from the same group as HAGE and MAGMA (Dongming Jiang, Yi Li, Bingzhe Li), so a trained-controller follow-up from them is likely.
errors.source: https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.23986 (full text https://arxiv.org/html/2609.23986, Appendix B); https://typesafe.ai/ ; https://huggingface.co/Contrastive-LM/CLM-v0.1-8B

errors.claim: CLM-8B row: 'Our bridge design, scaled down to a phone-size encoder'. Joint training: 'The state head then reads the LLM's own hidden state at every step' with a LoRA on the shared Qwen3-8B.
errors.correction: The facts in the row are right. CLM-8B has state and action heads on a frozen Qwen3-8B, trained with bidirectional InfoNCE, under Apache 2.0. The Hugging Face repo was created 21 Sep 2026, and the stated limitations match the model card. Note that the model card lists the authors (Kwok, Kang, Suresh, Saad-Falcon, Pavone, Ré, Mirhoseini) without affiliations; 'Stanford + NVIDIA' comes from press coverage. Two overstatements follow from the card itself. (1) The heads are 'encoder-locked' to Qwen3-8B last-token-pooled embeddings. None of CLM's pre-, mid- and post-training (about 60M pairs, about 30M hard negatives, about 1M agentic trajectories) carries over to bge-small bridges: those are new heads trained from scratch with the same kind of loss. (2) CLM's state head reads a pooled embedding of the state text from the frozen base model, not the generating model's per-step hidden state. LoRA-tuning that same backbone would shift the embeddings the heads are locked to, and would make stale any key computed from that backbone.

errors.claim: LoCoMo audit (2026) row: 'Its LLM judge accepted up to 63% of deliberately wrong answers; about 6% of gold answers are wrong' — fix: 'We score retrieval of marked evidence, not a judge.'
errors.correction: The numbers are right, but the source is not a paper. It is a Penfield Labs blog post (DEV and Substack, 4 Apr 2026) with a GitHub repo (dial481/locomo-audit). The figures: 99 of 1,540 non-adversarial questions (6.4%) have score-corrupting gold-answer errors, and the gpt-4o-mini judge accepted 62.81% of deliberately wrong 'vague-but-topical' answers (specific factual errors were caught about 89% of the time). The row leaves out a finding that bears directly on the page's fix. The same audit found 57 more WRONG_CITATION errors, where the evidence dialog IDs do not support the answer, plus 4 malformed evidence IDs. The marked evidence the page scores and trains on is therefore itself wrong for about 4% of questions. The fix moves the label noise; it does not remove it. The audit also argues that LongMemEval-S (about 115K tokens per question) fits in a modern context window, which bears on using it as the second benchmark.

errors.claim: Titans, TTT-E2E (2025) row: 'An independent re-implementation found mixed results tied to chunking; no original code.'
errors.correction: The row mixes the two papers. Both points apply only to Titans (Behrouz et al., arXiv 31 Dec 2024). The re-implementation (Di Nepi et al., arXiv 2510.09551) tested masked language modelling, time series and recommendation, not large-scale language modelling. It found Titans 'does not always outperform established baselines due to chunking', while its neural memory consistently beat attention-only models. TTT-E2E (Tandon et al., arXiv 29 Dec 2025) has public code. Its own reported weaknesses are that full attention 'dramatically outperforms' it on RULER needle-in-a-haystack (its recall is lossy) and that training latency is 'a significant limitation'.
errors.source: https://arxiv.org/abs/2510.09551 ; https://arxiv.org/abs/2501.00663 ; https://arxiv.org/abs/2512.23675 (section 3.5 and the latency section of https://arxiv.org/html/2512.23675v2)

errors.claim: REALM, RAG, Atlas row: problem 'Index goes stale when the encoder trains; re-embedding everything is costly' — fix 'Encoder frozen; only the heads train.'
errors.correction: The stale-index problem is real for REALM, which refreshes its index asynchronously. RAG already avoided it: Lewis et al. 'keep the document encoder (and index) fixed, only fine-tuning the query encoder and the BART generator'. Atlas explicitly evaluates 'query-side fine-tuning' with a fixed document encoder and no re-indexing. So the page's fix is the standard RAG/Atlas workaround, not a new answer. Atlas also warns that the effect of fixing the document encoder 'varies greatly for different tasks' when there is plenty of training data, which suggests heads-only training may cap the gains.
errors.source: https://arxiv.org/abs/2005.11401 (section 2.4); https://arxiv.org/abs/2208.03299 (section on efficient retriever fine-tuning, 'Query-side fine-tuning')

errors.claim: Memory Networks, NTM, DNC row: 'Fully differentiable memory read and written by a network.'
errors.correction: Minor. The original Memory Networks (Weston et al., 2014) used hard argmax addressing and were trained with strong supervision on the supporting facts. Only End-to-End Memory Networks (Sukhbaatar et al., 2015), NTM and DNC are fully differentiable. 'Never scaled' is an opinion, not a finding.

errors.claim: Complementary learning systems row: problem it hit 'Interference when the fast store writes into the slow one.'
errors.correction: Minor. In McClelland, McNaughton and O'Reilly (1995), catastrophic interference is the problem the theory explains and solves, not a problem it ran into. Interference arises if the slow neocortical system learns new items quickly and without interleaving. The hippocampus avoids this by storing fast and replaying into the neocortex gradually and interleaved.

missing.title: In Prospect and Retrospect: Reflective Memory Management for Long-term Personalized Dialogue Agents (RMM)
missing.what: It adds residual linear query and memory heads on top of a frozen retriever (Contriever or GTE) and trains them online with REINFORCE and Gumbel top-k sampling, using the generator LLM's own per-memory citations as reward (+1 cited, -1 not cited), over a memory organised at the utterance, turn and session levels.
missing.bearing: It already does the core of the page's backward pass (small heads on a frozen encoder, trained from the reasoner's cites, with unused reads as negatives), so the gap claim must be narrowed. It also reports two useful lessons: updating the retriever directly with RL rather than through a small head hurt results (forgetting), and the cite labels proved valid (high precision and recall against a Gemini judge).

missing.title: Retrieval-Driven Memory Reconsolidation for Long-Term LLM Agents (REALM)
missing.what: After each query, an agent rewires the activated subgraph of a heterogeneous memory graph (adding, removing and retyping edges) using the retrieval and answer feedback, which gives +2.0 on LoCoMo and +2.1 on LongMemEval, with the largest gains on multi-hop.
missing.bearing: This is already a 'memory that learns its own structure from use'. The difference is that REALM does it by prompting an LLM, not with learned reshape heads, so the page's learned reshape and write bridges must be compared against it and must beat it.

missing.title: The Retriever Should Remember: Experience-Amortized Reranking for Long-Term Agent Memory (EARM)
missing.what: It stores the LLM's past query-to-memory relevance scores in an online matrix and fills in the missing scores by causal matrix completion, so the retriever keeps getting better over the agent's lifetime with fewer LLM calls.
missing.bearing: It is a direct alternative to the page's per-ask alias keys as a way for memory to remember how it proved useful. It is a natural baseline for the 'keys learn from cites' result.

missing.title: MemRL: Self-Evolving Agents via Runtime Reinforcement Learning on Episodic Memory (also see Memento, arXiv 2508.16153)
missing.what: The LLM stays frozen. Each memory entry carries a learned utility (Q-value), updated from task reward whenever the entry is used, and retrieval is a semantic filter followed by ranking on that Q-value. Memento likewise learns a neural case-selection policy online over a frozen LLM.
missing.bearing: This is prior art for a per-node quantity that learns from use while the reasoner stays frozen, close to the page's residual r_v. REALM's authors criticise MemRL for optimising isolated entries without changing structure, which is the same line the page draws.

missing.title: Organize then Retrieve: Hierarchical Memory Navigation for Efficient Agents (HORMA)
missing.what: It keeps memory as a hierarchy, like a file system, of summaries linked to raw trajectories. A lightweight navigator (Qwen 3.5 4B) is trained with GRPO on an evidence-overlap reward to fetch the minimal context. It is evaluated on LoCoMo, LongMemEval and ALFWorld.
missing.bearing: It is the closest learned router over a pyramid-like hierarchy, though its navigator still generates text. It explicitly flags the credit-assignment gap when memory construction and retrieval are trained jointly from task reward, which is the risk in the page's EM-style alternation.

missing.title: MAGMA: A Multi-Graph based Agentic Memory Architecture for AI Agents
missing.what: It stores memory as orthogonal semantic, temporal, causal and entity graphs and retrieves by policy-guided traversal.
missing.bearing: It is the memory plane that both HAGE and Jev-Mem build on, from the same group, which has moved from MAGMA (Jan) to HAGE (May, learned) to Jev-Mem (Sep, System-One controller). A trained System-One controller is the obvious next paper from them, so it is a scooping risk.

missing.title: REPLUG: Retrieval-Augmented Black-Box Language Models (REPLUG LSR)
missing.what: It trains the retriever from the feedback of a frozen black-box LM, aligning the retrieval distribution with how much each document lowers the LM's perplexity.
missing.bearing: It is the canonical way to train a retriever from a frozen API reasoner, which is the page's stage 1 with Claude or Haiku. It is a softer, denser alternative signal to binary cites and should be cited and compared.

missing.title: Augmenting Language Models with Long-Term Memory (LongMem)
missing.what: The backbone LLM is frozen and used as the memory encoder, and a trainable residual side network acts as the memory retriever and reader, explicitly to avoid memory staleness.
missing.bearing: It is precedent for stage 3, where bridges read the LLM's hidden states. It shows why the backbone was kept frozen: if a LoRA changes the backbone that keys or states come from, cached memory goes stale. The page's joint LoRA plan reintroduces that problem.

missing.title: Agent Memory as Recommendation: Recommender-System Design for Long-Term Memory of LLM Agents (AgentMemRec); also ConvMemory, arXiv 2605.28062
missing.what: It uses an LLM-free cascade (candidate generation, a LightGBM LambdaRank ranker trained on gold evidence labels, budgeted slate fill), reports +10 to 31 points over A-Mem, HippoRAG 2 and others on LongMemEval multi-session, and beats Mem0 and Zep on LoCoMo. ConvMemory is a 3.6M-parameter learned reranker whose claimed temporal mechanism failed a five-seed ablation.
missing.bearing: Both are strong, cheap learned-ranking baselines that the bridges must beat to count as proof. ConvMemory's negative attribution result is a warning that a gain from a learned head can be plain distillation, not the claimed mechanism, so the page's 'each part earns its place' ablation plan needs the same rigour.

missing.title: Query association for effective retrieval (Scholer and Williams); see also Document Expansion by Query Prediction (doc2query, arXiv 1904.08375)
missing.what: It stores past queries alongside the documents they retrieved and uses those query associations as document surrogates or expansions. Doc2query predicts such queries with a sequence-to-sequence model.
missing.bearing: Per-ask alias keys are a learned-embedding version of query association, an IR technique more than 20 years old. It should be cited, and its known failure modes (associations drifting onto popular documents, the need to cap associations per document) apply directly.

missing.title: Unbiased Learning-to-Rank with Biased Feedback
missing.what: It shows that implicit feedback such as clicks is biased by position and exposure, and corrects for this with propensity-weighted counterfactual learning.
missing.bearing: Cites only ever come from what the read bridge opened in the top 10, so training on them is exposure-biased: nodes that were never opened can never become positives. That is a rich-get-richer loop the page should plan for with propensity weighting or exploration.

missing.title: Adversarial Hubness in Multi-Modal Retrieval
missing.what: It shows that hubness in high-dimensional embedding spaces lets a single crafted item become the top result for thousands of unrelated queries.
missing.bearing: Nodes that accumulate many alias keys under a max or softmax over keys will naturally turn into hubs. A hostile message that gets cited could also be planted as an adversarial hub, so per-node alias caps, hubness monitoring and CSLS-style normalisation belong next to the page's 'walls' rule.

result.novelty_judgment: The claimed gap is real but much narrower than the page says, and most of its parts already exist. RMM (ACL 2025) has small heads on a frozen encoder trained from the reasoner's own cites, with uncited reads as negatives. HAGE (May 2026) learns structure and a router from downstream evidence reward on frozen MiniLM embeddings, under the same held-out-conversation LoCoMo protocol. REALM (Sep 2026) changes memory topology after each use. MemRL and EARM keep per-memory usefulness that learns over time. Jev-Mem (Sep 2026) is the three-plane System-One architecture itself, and because CLM-8B exposes Jev's typed API as open weights, making Jev-Mem's controller open and fine-tunable is close to a drop-in swap. Per-ask alias keys are a learned form of query association (2002). What no one appears to have published as of 27 Oct 2026 is the specific combination: CLM-style contrastive (InfoNCE) state and action heads used as one family of read, stop, write, reshape and forget decisions; learned rather than prompted topology operations; per-node keys updated per ask; a read-again loop driven by the reasoner's thoughts; and, at stage 3, joint LoRA training with heads that read the reasoner's hidden states. That is a solid, publishable systems combination, not a new paradigm. Two things make it weaker today. First, the current results train on LoCoMo's gold evidence ('oracle cites'), which is HAGE's supervision signal; per the Penfield audit those labels are wrong for about 4% of questions. Second, the MAGMA, HAGE and Jev-Mem group is visibly one step away from a trained System-One controller. The claim becomes defensible once real Haiku or Claude cites replace the gold evidence and the bridges beat RMM-style cite-trained heads, HAGE, REALM and an LLM-free learned-to-rank baseline (AgentMemRec) on held-out data. The rows I checked and found accurate: Does memory need graphs? (ACL 2026 long paper 2026.acl-long.1232; it evaluates on LongMemEval and HaluMem, not LoCoMo); Memory-R1 (Aug 2025; PPO and GRPO with 152 QA pairs); AgeMem (Jan 2026, ACL'26; step-wise GRPO for sparse rewards); RETRO; Jev-Mem's 0.777 score; and the CLM-8B architecture and license.
result.closest_work: RMM, Reflective Memory Management (Tan et al., ACL 2025, https://arxiv.org/abs/2503.08026), is the closest match for the backward pass: small residual heads on a frozen retriever, trained online from the answering LLM's own citations with cited as positive and uncited as negative. Close behind are HAGE (https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.09942), which learns graph-edge structure and a router from evidence reward and is cross-validated on held-out LoCoMo conversations, and Jev-Mem (https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.23986), which is the three-plane System-One architecture with a zero-shot closed controller. REALM (https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.16053) is the closest for structure learned from use, though its rewiring is done by prompting an LLM.
